entries.english:
Co-plaintiffs/applicants/intervenors: Bernhard and Georg (Ludwig) von Hutten zu Frankenberg, Michelfeld, and Birkenfeld, brothers.
Co-defendants/intervenors: Wolf Dietrich, Seifried, Alexander, and Veit von Stein zum Altenstein zu Maroldsweisach, Pfarrweisach, and Altenstein; Hans Ludwig von Seckendorf zu Sugenheim; Achaz von Giech on behalf of Sabina von Stein zum Altenstein, née von Hutten; Joachim Fuchs von Wonfurt zu Rügheim for his wife Sibylla, née von Stein zum Altenstein; Philipp Jakob von und zu Thüngen for his wife Agatha, née von Seckendorff; and Eva von Lichtenstein zu Geiersberg, née von Hutten, for her sons Sebastian and Hans von Lichtenstein.

Counsel for the plaintiffs and defendants changed over the course of the proceedings; the record lists their names and appointments from 1576 through 1747 for the plaintiffs and from 1583 through 1745 for the defendants.

Contemporary subject of dispute: *simplex querela*. Modern subject: dispute over a family inheritance agreement. The plaintiffs rely on an inheritance agreement concluded in 1498 by the brothers Ludwig, Konrad, and Hans von Hutten, which their father Konrad von Hutten also recognized and confirmed by testament. They argue that it established inheritance in the male line, while female descendants were entitled only to a marriage portion of no more than 1,500 florins, and that the agreement created a family entail. Contrary to its provisions, several family members appointed female descendants as heirs, transferring family property into other hands. The plaintiffs seek recognition of the agreement, restitution of former Hutten property, and damages.

The defendants seek a declaration that the 1498 agreement is void and reimbursement of their litigation costs. They argue that it did not create an entail and that Hans von Hutten himself had already acted against it in his testamentary dispositions. They further maintain that descendants of the brothers violated the agreement and, by consenting to later arrangements—including the 1548 Eichstätt agreement mediated by Moritz von Hutten, Bischof zu Eichstätt, and the 1569 Kitzingen agreement between Veit von Lichtenstein zu Geiersberg and Bernhard von Hutten—recognized that the 1498 agreement was void.

In 1744 the Imperial Chamber Court ruled that the agreement did not establish an entail and absolved the defendants; the parties were to settle the costs. A plaintiffs’ petition for restitution was rejected in 1761, and the plaintiffs were ordered to reimburse the opposing party’s costs. Proceedings: Imperial Chamber Court, 1583–1763 (recorded span 1583–1795).

The files include the 1473 partition agreement of Konrad von Hutten; the 1498 inheritance agreement of the brothers Ludwig, Konrad, and Hans; related undertakings and testaments (1500–1517); the 1548–1549 Eichstätt inheritance agreement; the 1569 Kitzingen agreement; marriage, partition, renunciation, purchase, and settlement contracts and related correspondence (1450–1735); extracts from contracts, property descriptions, rent books, and the Ippesheim fief register (1533–1669); legal opinions and pleadings (including a 1739 printed brief); family trees and descriptions of Hutten kinship and marriage contracts; and an engraving of Asbach manor and castle (c. 1750).

File notes: Register records the start of proceedings as 1583. Prior opinions/venues include Dr. iur. Georg Adalbert Burckhard (d. 1618), and Leipzig, Marburg an der Lahn, Wittenberg, and Würzburg.

The plaintiffs’ counsel over the proceedings were Dr. Bernhard Küehorn (1576), Dr. Sebastian Wolf (1602), Dr. Johann Georg Krapf (1614), Lic. Christian Christoph Dimpfel with substitute Dr. Johann Nikolaus Schmidt (1717), Schmidt with substitute Dr. Johann Heinrich Dietz (1726), Schmidt with substitute Lic. Johann Melchior Deuren (1733), Schmidt with substitute Dr. Georg Samuel Scheffer (1737), Dr. Johann Paul Besserer with substitute Dr. Georg Melchior Hofmann (1738), and Dr. Johann Albert Ruland with substitute Lic. Jakob Loskant (1747). Defendants’ counsel were Dr. Paul Buchner (1583), Lic. Jakob Erhardt (1585), Dr. Laurentius Vomelius Stapert (1589), Lic. Hartmann Cogmann and Dr. Marsilius Bergner (1593), Dr. Werner Bontz (1599), Dr. Konrad Fabri (1601), Dr. Andreas Pfeffer (1602), Dr. Leonhard Wolf (1604), Lic. Peter Paul Steurnagel (1623), Dr. Cornelius Lindheimer with substitute Dr. Christian Hartmann von Gülich (1716), Dr. Johann Goy with substitute Lic. Johann Peter Thonet and Dr. Christian Hartmann von Gülich with substitute Dr. Johann Jakob Wahl (1718), Lic. Johann Justus Faber (1724), Dr. Johann Paul Besserer with substitute Dr. Georg Melchior Hofmann (1729), Faber with substitute von Gülich (1730), Goy with substitute Dr. Johann Wilhelm Ludolf (1737), and Ludolf with substitute Dr. Johann Ludwig Pfeiffer (1745).

The records include Konrad von Hutten’s 1473 partition agreement; the 1498 inheritance agreement of Ludwig, Konrad, and Hans von Hutten; Bernhard von Hutten’s 1500 undertaking to observe it; Konrad and Hans von Hutten’s wills (1500–1505) and an extract from Ludwig’s will (1517); and Ludwig’s 1507 partition of the estate of his brother Hans. They also include the 1548–1549 Eichstätt partition agreement among Konrad von Hutten, his sister Eva von Lichtenstein, and their sisters Margaretha von Seckendorf and Sabina von Stein zum Altenstein; a 1672 Ippesheim estate agreement among Philipp Gottfried, Graf zu Castell, Rosina Sibylla Fuchs von Wallburg, née von Lichtenstein, Louisa Sophia von Schlammersdorf, and Dietrich von Streitberg; and a 1673 supplemental agreement about usufruct of Asbachhof between Hans Georg von Lichtenstein’s heirs and his widow Helena Maria, née von Stetten.

Other attachments include Veit Ulrich von Schaumberg zu Thundorf and Hans von Selbitz zu Einöd’s 1556 protest as the plaintiffs’ guardians concerning the obligation imposed on Ippesheim subjects in favor of Veit von Lichtenstein; Georg Ludwig von Hutten’s protest against the 1569 Kitzingen agreement (1569, 1571); and the Kitzingen agreement between Veit von Lichtenstein and Bernhard von Hutten zu Frankenberg exchanging vogt jurisdiction and grazing rights at Ippesheim and half the tithe at Reusch (1569). Renunciation deeds include Anna (Margaretha) von Eltershofen, née von Seckendorff, relinquishing claims to her father Hans Ludwig von Seckendorf’s estate in favor of her brothers Hans Georg and Gottfried (1593); Margaretha von Heßberg, née von Hutten, and Anna von Hutten concerning their paternal inheritance (1523); and Agnes von Schaumberg, Anna von Thüngen, Margaretha Truchseß von Wetzhausen, Anna von Vellberg, and Anna Fuchs von Bimbach zu Burgpreppach, all née von Hutten, renouncing claims to their fathers’ estates (1458–1521). A 1505 contract by Ernst von Waldenfels zu Lichtenberg as guardian for Margaretha and Anna von Hutten, daughters of Hans, together with their mother Barbara, née von Waldenfels, Ludwig, and Konrad von Hutten, covers renunciation of their paternal inheritance and the widow’s portion. Marriage contracts concern Zaisolph von Rosenberg zu Haltenbergstetten and Ursula von Hutten, sister of Ulrich, Ludwig, and Hans (1508); Wilhelm von Grumbach zu Rimpar and Anna, daughter of Hans von Hutten (1524); and Ursula von Hutten and (Georg) Siegmund von Adelsheim (1565). Other material includes Konrad von Hutten’s 1550 release-and-assignment deed for properties at Schernau, Euerfeld, Arnstein, Hirschfeld, and Obbach; correspondence of Valentin Friedrich and Hans Ernst von Hutten with an imperial commission concerning Hutten rights at the sequestered manor of Schernau (1674); letters from Wilhelm von Grumbach, Hans Georg von Heßberg, and Moritz, Bischof zu Eichstätt about the Eichstätt agreement (1549); and correspondence between Ernst von Waldenfels, Ludwig von Hutten, and Schweinfurt’s mayor and council about delivery of documents (1505). The file also contains opposing parties’ correspondence about a 1,000-florin principal and a pledge of ten acres of meadow at Asbach (1633–1634).

Further estate documents include the 1701 sale of two thirds of Ippesheim manor by Georg Eberhard von Limpurg-Speckfeld to Johann Friedrich, Graf zu Castell; 1676–1706 sale agreements concerning Asbach manor among Albrecht Ludwig von Ostheim, brothers Christian Ernst and Johann Georg von Reichenbach, and Georg Holzschuher von Neuenburg; sales concerning Frankenberg manor (1450–1520); and sales by Konrad and Hans von Bernheim and Hans von Absberg of two farms at Asbach (1458–1471). Extracts from contracts, property descriptions, rent and dues books, and the Ippesheim fief register date from 1533–1669. The collection further contains an undated Hutten family tree spanning the fifteenth through eighteenth centuries; an undated agreement between Konrad and his brother Bartholomäus von Hutten concerning male-line succession; legal opinions from Leipzig and Wittenberg on the inheritance rights of Margaretha von Heßberg and Anna von Grumbach, daughters of Hans von Hutten; Georg Adalbert Burckhard’s printed opinion for the case, confirmed by Marburg’s law faculty and accompanied by a fifteenth- or sixteenth-century Hutten family tree (c. 1743), and Würzburg’s law faculty’s confirmation of Burckhard’s opinion (1616); and an undated account of Hutten kinship and marriage agreements through the 1548 Eichstätt agreement. Other exhibits are a contingent 1533 agreement between Markgraf Georg von Brandenburg-Ansbach und Brandenburg-Kulmbach and Ludwig von Hutten concerning Hutten allodial and fief property; charters of Konrad, Ludwig, and Bernhard von Hutten depositing documents with Schweinfurt’s mayor and council (1501–1530); the 1735 decree of the Odenwald canton of the Franconian Knighthood concerning Asbach manor; a printed 1739 brief, *Geschichts- und Actenmäßige Species facti in causa Von Hutten Contra Altenstein-Lichtenstein*; and an engraving of Asbach manor and castle (c. 1750). The register gives 1583 as the start of the proceedings. Prior venues were the fief court at Schleusingen and the fief court at Wiesenbronn; Dr. Georg Adalbert Burckhard (d. 1618) is listed as a legal opinion writer. The listed prior institutions are Leipzig, Marburg an der Lahn, Wittenberg, and Würzburg.
